source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023/2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: GPT-3.5 does worse on n-back as n rises from 1 to 3. The authors say the drop near n=3 matches the human limit.
numbers: Verbal n-back, n=1,2,3, 50 blocks per condition. In three of four verbal variants d' falls to about 1 at n=3. Adding noise symbols lowers capacity further. Chain-of-thought raised spatial n-back scores.
limits: Behavioural match only. Hu and Lewis (b04) show low scores can come from task misunderstanding. No human control group; the human curve is taken from Jaeggi 2010.
agent_relevance: A drop at n=3 is not proof of a storage limit. Do not copy 'four slots' into the schema from this paper alone.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023/2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: Several models (Bloomz, ChatGLM, Vicuna, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) were compared on the base verbal n-back. The authors propose n-back as a benchmark of model working memory.
numbers: Models compared at n=1,2,3 with 30 blocks each; results shown only as a figure (Figure 9), no table, so no exact scores recorded.
limits: Letter streams of 24 items only. The authors say span tasks are still untested.
agent_relevance: If we measure the agent's own state tracking, use a graded load test and report d', not raw accuracy.

source: Gong and Zhang (2024) Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
finding: Small decoder-only transformers trained on n-back lose accuracy as n grows. Spread of attention (higher entropy) goes with the loss.
numbers: Layers L in {1,2}, heads H in {1,2,4}, N up to 6. Kruskal-Wallis H=38.517, p<.001, eta-squared=0.248 for the effect of N. Log-like decline in test accuracy. Larger models stayed above 95% at all N.
limits: Toy models trained from scratch. Later work (b06) finds a second layer removes the attention bottleneck, so this account is partial.
agent_relevance: Bigger models lose less, so a scaffold may matter most for small or cheap models.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? Investigations with the N-Back Paradigm
finding: Challenges Gong et al. Low n-back scores in weaker models come partly from not understanding the task and from losing the task rule over the stream, not only from a capacity limit.
numbers: Three performance tiers across open models. Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct retrieval accuracy 0.99 at 2-back and 0.62 (sd .31) at 3-back. Gemma-2-27B 0.61 and 0.31. Qwen-1.5-14B-Chat failed to get two correct answers in a row after 10 demos.
quote: we show that the poor performance is due at least in part to a limitation in task comprehension and task set maintenance
limits: Open models only (6B-70B). The attention analysis (best matching pattern 71.98% in Qwen, 8.52% in Llama-70B) is a hint, not proof.
agent_relevance: A failed working-memory probe may be a failed instruction. Check the task rule is still held at the end of a long run.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025)
finding: With a curriculum of easier n-back demos, the best model succeeds far beyond the supposed human-like limit of 3, up to 10-back.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B: exact-letter retrieval 75.25%, 66.08%, 57.1% at n=8,9,10; task accuracy 90.08%, 90.08%, 84.75% at n=8,9,10.
limits: One model. Shows the n=3 break point in b01 depends on prompting, not on a fixed cap.
agent_relevance: Do not design the schema around a fixed 'capacity of 3'. A model's capacity depends on how the task is taught.

source: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory (2026)
finding: Tests two rival accounts of the LLM n-back limit: attention precision versus interference. Results favour interference. Attention lands on the target even on missed matches, yet the answer is wrong.
numbers: 15 pretrained LLMs from 3 families, 70M to 14B parameters. Linear probes decode near perfectly whether a match was at the target or at a lure, even on false alarms. In GPT-2 at N=3 probe AUC falls to 0.84-0.89 by the last layer. Sharpening attention gave negligible gains. Suppressing letter identity of non-target items raised d' in nearly all model-by-load cells.
limits: Small and mid-size open models; frontier models not tested. Single paper.
agent_relevance: The information is in the model; reading it out under competing items fails. Remove competing items from the prompt rather than asking the model to try harder.

source: In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in large language models (2026)
finding: A two-layer transformer solves a working memory task perfectly, but diverse trained LLMs decline with load, show recency bias and lure effects, as humans do. Multiple memories sit in entangled form. A causal intervention that suppresses interfering content improves performance.
numbers: Lures: with probability 0.25 the current input repeats an N-1 item. Table 1 reports Pearson r between each interference manipulation and accuracy pooled over models and N (values -.51, .36, -.32, -.30, -.26, -.62; column labels not fully readable in the text extract). WM performance tracks broader model capability.
limits: Correlational across models; mechanism shown on open models only.
agent_relevance: Interference between simultaneously active items is the likely limit, as in human SOB models. Keep the number of live, similar items small.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length (PI-LLM)
finding: Streams of key-value updates, asking only for the last value. Retrieval accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as earlier values pile up. Errors are the old values. This holds with input length held constant.
numbers: Update counts 3 to 400 (log-spaced), 46 keys. One model group reached 0% at 400 updates per key. Model size class predicts interference resistance (t=3.03, p=0.005, N=30 models); context length does not (t=-0.144, p=0.886); R-squared 0.261. Among models with 128k-131k context, Spearman rho=0.673, p=0.0016, N=19.
limits: Synthetic key-value task. Humans are described as accurate, but no human data were collected in this paper.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an agent which keeps appending revisions to one variable will read stale values. Overwrite or delete state in code; do not rely on the model to ignore old text.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget
finding: Telling the model in plain words to ignore earlier values, or asking it to restate the task goal first, helped only a little. The authors call this missing top-down control.
numbers: Natural-language annotations marking prior values as outdated gave limited gains. Some models show a step-like capacity collapse, others a gradual log-linear decline.
limits: Few prompt variants tried. Single study.
agent_relevance: Supports our rule that the program removes stale state; the model is not asked to forget.

source: Strong Memory, Weak Control: An Empirical Study of Executive Functioning in LLMs (2025)
finding: Six open models (Gemma2, Llama3.1, Qwen2, two sizes each) beat typical human scores on simple spans and lead by less on complex spans, but are below humans on executive tasks. More span did not go with better executive or problem-solving scores.
numbers: Wisconsin Card Sorting, 3060 trials per model (102 trials x 30 prompts): accuracy Llama3.1-8B 0.29, Llama3.1-70B 0.49, Qwen2-7B 0.53, Qwen2-72B 0.50; humans typically 0.70-0.80 (healthy adult row in their table 0.51-0.77 groups for error types). Digit span tested at 15 and 50 digits against human span of 5 to 7.
limits: Human norms are rough estimates from other studies. Two groups of models, open weights only.
agent_relevance: Raw store size is not the limit. The weak part is control: inhibition, switching, keeping a rule. Put those in code (states, counters), not in the model.

source: Vision versus text in working memory: Spatial n-Back in Vision-Language Models (2026)
finding: Qwen2.5 and Qwen2.5-VL do better on text-rendered grids than on image-rendered grids. Nominal 2- and 3-back often behaves like a recency-locked comparison, not the instructed lag.
numbers: Models show reliably higher accuracy and d' with text. Grid size changes how often recent repeats occur, shifting interference and error patterns.
limits: Small open models; spatial task only.
agent_relevance: Pass state as text, not pictures. Check that a probe measures what you asked; a lag-n test may be solved by a shortcut.

source: United Minds or Isolated Agents? Exploring Coordination of LLMs under Cognitive Load Theory (CoThinker, TMLR 2026)
finding: A multi-agent design that splits load and keeps a shared working memory helps on reasoning-heavy tasks, and coordination cost dominates on low-load tasks such as instruction following.
numbers: Tested on Gemini-1.5-Flash-8B, Flash and Pro with LiveBench and CommonGen-Hard plus fabricated high-load cases. Exact gains not extracted.
limits: Cognitive Load Theory is a design analogy, not a validated mechanism for LLMs. Several agents from one model are not independent (our G4).
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: extra structure helps only when task load is high. Fits our rule to use the heavy scaffold on hard items only.

source: Soveri, Antfolk, Karlsson, Salo, Laine (2017) Working memory training revisited: a multi-level meta-analysis of n-back training studies
finding: n-back training raises performance on untrained n-back tasks by a medium amount and on other transfer domains by very little.
numbers: 33 randomized controlled studies, 203 effect sizes (190 after screening), 2,105 individuals. Untrained n-back g=0.62 [0.44,0.81]; other working-memory tasks g=0.24 [0.16,0.32]; cognitive control g=0.16 [0.05,0.27]; fluid intelligence g=0.16 [0.08,0.24]. Moderator test QM(3)=23.77, p<.001.
limits: Older meta-analyses folded untrained versions of the trained task into 'WM', which inflated them.
agent_relevance: Training a skill moves the trained skill. Tuning an agent on n-back-like probes would not be expected to lift its reasoning.

source: Soveri et al. (2017)
finding: No effect of age, training dose, single versus dual n-back, or verbal versus visuospatial stimuli on transfer. Active versus passive control did not differ within experiments.
numbers: Training dose g=0.01 [-0.12,0.14], p=.87; single vs dual g=0.06 [-0.05,0.18]; active vs passive control g=0.09 [-0.03,0.21], p=.13. Single n-back training g=0.27 [0.18,0.37]; dual n-back g=0.18 [0.11,0.26]. Residual heterogeneity QE(186)=230.59, p<.05.
limits: Samples mostly young adults. Heterogeneity stayed significant.
agent_relevance: More practice gave no more transfer. Do not expect extra loops of the same drill to generalise.

source: Au, Buschkuehl, Duncan, Jaeggi (2016) There is no convincing evidence that working memory training is NOT effective: reply to Melby-Lervag and Hulme
finding: A dispute over whether n-back training raises fluid intelligence. Au et al. found g=0.24; Melby-Lervag and Hulme's re-analysis found 0.13, which lost significance without active controls. Au et al. argue control-group type is not a real moderator.
numbers: Original Au et al. 2015 g=0.24; Melby-Lervag and Hulme baseline-corrected g=0.13. The reply tests several effect-size methods and reaffirms the original result.
limits: Same trials, different coding choices give different answers. Soveri 2017 later found fluid-intelligence g=0.16.
agent_relevance: Effects near 0.1 to 0.25 depend on analysis choices. Treat transfer claims as small and unsettled.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Working memory training in typically developing children: a meta-analysis of the available evidence
finding: In children, training raises WM-related skills moderately, but far transfer is tiny and vanishes in the best-designed studies.
limits: Typically developing children aged 3 to 16 only.
agent_relevance: Gains shrink as design quality rises.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017)
finding: Design quality moderates far transfer. Randomized studies with an active control group show no effect.
numbers: Random allocation moderator b=-0.20, p=.006: randomized g=0.07 [0.00,0.14] (k=50), non-randomized g=0.27 [0.15,0.39] (k=24). Active control g=0.05 [-0.05,0.15] (k=40); passive g=0.18 [0.09,0.26] (k=34). Randomized and active-control g=0.03 [-0.07,0.14] (k=34). Age b=-0.03 p=.110; domain p=.703; duration b=-0.02 p=.070.
limits: Moderators are confounded across studies.
agent_relevance: When we claim a scaffold helps, compare with an active control (plain model, same compute), not a weak baseline.

source: Cowan (2010) The Magical Mystery Four: How is Working Memory Capacity Limited, and Why?
finding: Capacity is about 3 to 5 chunks when rehearsal and grouping are blocked. Miller's older 7 came from chunking and rehearsal. Young adults recall only 3 or 4 longer verbal chunks.
numbers: Central limit 3 to 5 meaningful items in young adults. About 2 seconds of speech can be held by silent rehearsal. In running span only the last 3 to 5 digits are recalled. Gilchrist, Cowan and Naveh-Benjamin 2008: 3 to 4 chunks for idioms or short sentences.
limits: Review by the main proponent, not an independent test. Resource view in b21.
agent_relevance: The count of items in an agent's active set matters after chunking. Group related facts into named chunks and keep few chunks live.

source: Rouder, Morey, Cowan, Zwilling, Morey, Pratte (2008) An assessment of fixed-capacity models of visual working memory
finding: Change-detection ROC curves were straight lines with slope 1.0, as an all-or-none fixed-slot model predicts. The fixed-capacity model beat variable-capacity rivals.
numbers: 23 students. Array sizes 2, 5, 8; change probability 0.3, 0.5, 0.7; 60-trial blocks. Fixed-capacity model: chance an item is in memory is k/M.
limits: Colour squares with well separated colours only. Some individuals violated the model. Small sample.
agent_relevance: Slot-like all-or-none storage is supported for simple, well-separated items. Agent facts are not like that.

source: Rouder et al. (2008)
finding: Earlier slot evidence was weak: an asymptote of capacity estimates at 3 to 4 items can be mimicked by models without fixed capacity. ROC lines are a stricter test.
numbers: Capacity estimates asymptote at 3 to 4 items for array sizes of 4 to 6 (Cowan's formula).
limits: Authors are slot-model proponents.
agent_relevance: Capacity numbers from a single formula are model-dependent; ask which model produced them.

source: Ma, Husain, Bays (2014) Changing concepts of working memory
finding: Review argues working memory is a limited resource shared flexibly (quality, not number of slots). Slot-model summary numbers like K or a guessing rate can mislead when the model is a poor description of the data.
numbers: Change-localization data were fitted by a variable-precision model with a Bayesian decision rule where the slot model was inadequate. Confidence ratings correlate strongly with accuracy, consistent with variable precision.
limits: Review by resource-view proponents. The rival slot view still fits some data (b19).
agent_relevance: Unequal precision across items means one prompt can hold some facts well and others poorly. Check which fact is dropped rather than count facts.

source: Lewandowsky, Geiger, Oberauer (2008) Interference-based forgetting in verbal short-term memory
finding: Four experiments: forgetting depends on how many different distractors are spoken, not on elapsed time. Repeating the same distractor caused no forgetting; several different ones did. Decay is hard to reconcile with this.
numbers: Experiment 1 used months of the year as distractors. Three-way interaction (between-burst similarity x number of distractors x within-burst similarity) F(1,22)=5.3, p=.03, partial eta-squared=.19 (df implies about 24 participants). Experiment 4 ruled out hidden attentional refreshing.
limits: Time-based resource-sharing and decay theorists report evidence for decay; the debate is not closed. Verbal materials only.
agent_relevance: Stale text hurts through interference, not through time passing. Reset by removing items, not by waiting.

source: Oberauer, Lewandowsky, Farrell, Jarrold, Greaves (2012) Modeling working memory: an interference model of complex span (SOB-CS)
finding: A two-layer network with overlapping position markers reproduces benchmark complex-span findings through interference. Free time between distractors is used to remove distractor traces. Refreshing is not needed in the model.
numbers: Removal of unwanted material takes 1 to 2 s in human experiments (rate parameter set to 1.5). Rival TBRS cognitive load CL = aN/T. Model covers four areas: pace/difficulty/steps; serial position and errors; similarity; span-task correlations. New predictions were confirmed in experiments.
limits: Model fit is not field-wide proof. TBRS (Barrouillet) predicts the same load effects with refreshing instead of removal.
agent_relevance: Clearing irrelevant bindings (explicit state resets) is the lever, rather than extra time.

source: Baddeley, Hitch, Allen (2019) From short-term store to multicomponent working memory: the role of the modal model
finding: Defends a separate short-term store against proposals that STM is just activated long-term memory, citing patients with grossly impaired LTM but intact STM and the reverse. Says Cowan's 1988 alternative reading of one patient has no evidence.
numbers: Atkinson and Shiffrin 1968 cited over 10,000 times by October 2018. Evidence is neuropsychological dissociation (Baddeley and Warrington 1970; Shallice and Warrington 1970; Vallar and Baddeley 1984).
limits: The authors are founders of the multicomponent model. Cowan's embedded-processes view competes; not settled.
agent_relevance: The rivals do not predict clearly different agent designs. Keep a small active set separate from the full store.

source: Turi, Alekseichuk, Paulus (2018) On ways to overcome the magical capacity limit of working memory (primer on Wolinski et al.)
finding: Primer on a brain-stimulation test of the theta-gamma coding account: changing the theta rhythm with tACS tests whether gamma cycles per theta cycle set the limit.
numbers: Theta 3 to 7 Hz, gamma above 25 Hz. No effect sizes in the text read.
limits: Primer, not the original trial. Brain stimulation effects on memory are often small and contested.
agent_relevance: None for the agent; records that a causal test of slot-style capacity exists in biology.

source: Redick et al. (2013) No evidence of intelligence improvement after working memory training: a randomized, placebo-controlled study
finding: Placebo-controlled adaptive training raised trained tasks but not fluid intelligence or other transfer measures (title and abstract as known; not opened this session).
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened. Verify numbers before use.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Soveri 2017 and Sala 2017: gains stay on the trained tasks.
